T4b threats (dormant backdoors embedded in model weights) are not detectable by this approach: the payload produces no behavioral anomaly until a specific trigger condition is met, at which point monitoring cannot distinguish the triggered response from intended behavior without knowledge of the trigger.

XI-F The Defense-in-Depth Principle for Agents

No single-layer defense is sufficient. Effective agentic security requires defense-in-depth: multiple independent controls at different layers, each covering the failure modes of the others. A minimal defense-in-depth stack for production agents:

  1. 1.

    L1+L4: Safety-trained model + tool output filtering

  2. 2.

    L3: Memory access control + write provenance tracking

  3. 3.

    L4+L6: Tool sandboxing + MCP server authentication

  4. 4.

    L5: Inter-agent message signing + behavioral correlation monitoring

  5. 5.

    L7: Comprehensive action logging + mandatory human review for irreversible actions

XII Evaluation Frameworks and Benchmarks

XII-A Benchmark Landscape

General-purpose LLM evaluation suites such as HELM [138] and TruthfulQA [139] measure accuracy and factuality but were not designed for adversarial security evaluation. Table IX surveys the current agent security benchmark landscape. Every benchmark in the table evaluates T1 or T2 threats. No security benchmark evaluates T3 or T4 threats, which means there is no way to measure whether defenses against slow-burn attacks improve over time. The three L7×\timesT4 entries in Table IV are alignment theory and governance papers, not evaluation frameworks, and do not contradict this finding.

XII-B Methodological Issues in Existing Evaluations

Beyond coverage gaps, we identify three methodological issues that limit the reliability of existing agent security evaluations:

Oblivious adversary assumption. Most evaluations test against a fixed attack strategy. Real adversaries adapt iteratively based on observed agent behavior. Adaptive attack evaluation, where the adversary is allowed to query the defended system and refine their attack before evaluation, yields substantially different (typically worse) defense performance.

No false positive reporting. Security evaluations consistently report attack mitigation rates (true positive rate for defense) but not false positive rates (i.e., rate at which the defense incorrectly flags legitimate agent behavior). A defense achieving 95% attack mitigation at 40% false positive rate is impractical; this information is absent from most published evaluations.

Single-agent evaluation for multi-agent threats. Benchmarks such as HarmBench and AgentHarm evaluate individual agents in isolation. They do not evaluate coordinated attacks against multi-agent systems, nor do they assess the spread of compromise through agent networks.

XII-C Evaluation Recommendations

We propose the following standards for rigorous agent security evaluation:

  1. 1.

    Report results under both oblivious and adaptive adversary settings.

  2. 2.

    For T3 evaluation, use multi-session protocols with ≥\geq5 session transitions between injection and exploitation.

  3. 3.

    Report false positive rates alongside true positive rates for all defenses.

  4. 4.

    Evaluate under heterogeneous agent deployments (mixed model families) for L5 threats.

  5. 5.

    Standardize threat model descriptions using the four-dimensional characterization from Section III.

XIII Research Gaps and Open Problems

The LASM ×\times temporality heatmap (Fig. 3) locates five research gaps in the high-risk, low-coverage zone.

XIV Future Directions

XIV-A Formal Security Models for Agentic Protocols

Cryptographic protocols achieve provable security via formal models (Dolev-Yao, universal composability). Agentic AI lacks analogous formal security models. Developing such models requires: (a) a formal language for specifying agent behavior and security properties; (b) a model of adversary capabilities in the agentic context; and (c) composition theorems allowing security proofs for complex multi-agent systems to be built from component proofs.

XIV-B Runtime Behavioral Attestation

A trusted execution environment for agent actions, providing cryptographic attestation that actions were sanctioned by a verified principal hierarchy, would address the accountability gap. Hardware trusted execution environments (Intel TDX, AMD SEV) provide the computational substrate; adapting them to the inference stack of LLM agents (stochastic, large memory footprint, streaming outputs) is a significant engineering challenge.

XIV-C Temporal Anomaly Detection Infrastructure

Addressing T3 and T4 threats requires building infrastructure that agents currently lack: (a) persistent, tamper-evident behavioral logs spanning multiple sessions; (b) statistical baselines for normal agent behavior specific to each deployment context; and (c) real-time anomaly scoring that can distinguish malicious behavioral shifts from legitimate adaptation. This is a systems research problem as much as an ML problem.

XIV-D Multi-Stakeholder Governance Frameworks

The distributed accountability chain (Section X) requires governance frameworks spanning developers, operators, users, and regulators. Legal frameworks assigning clear liability for agentic harms, analogous to product liability for physical goods, are an urgent policy priority as agentic AI deployments reach the scale at which harmful incidents become statistically inevitable.

XIV-E Closing the Defense Parity Gap

LLM agent teams can already autonomously exploit zero-day software vulnerabilities [99]. No analogous defensive capability exists: no agent system can autonomously defend against comparable threats. Developing defensive agents that autonomously detect, analyze, and mitigate attacks against themselves and their deployment environment is a long-term research objective requiring community coordination.

XV Comparison with Existing Surveys

Table X provides a systematic comparison of this survey with the six most closely related prior surveys.

XV-A Detailed Comparison

Wang et al. [14] organize security challenges around four knowledge gaps: unpredictability of multi-step inputs, complexity in internal executions, variability of operational environments, and interactions with untrusted external entities. This framing captures the sources of agent uncertainty but does not map to architectural components, making it difficult to derive defense placement decisions. Their coverage ends April 2024, predating MCP security, steganographic collusion benchmarks, and zero-day autonomous exploitation by agent teams.

Chhabra et al. [15] survey agentic AI security with a focus on evaluation benchmarks and governance frameworks. Their taxonomy distinguishes prompt injection, jailbreaks, autonomous exploitation, and multi-agent threats. Relative to our work, they lack the LASM layer decomposition, the temporality dimension, and detailed treatment of memory layer attacks and ecosystem supply-chain threats.

Tang et al. [16] propose a structure-aware taxonomy with three paradigms: External Interaction Attacks, Internal Cognitive Attacks, and Multi-Agent Collaboration Attacks. This is the closest in spirit to our layer decomposition, but it conflates L3 (memory) and L4 (tool) within “Internal” attacks and does not separate L6 (ecosystem) from L4. The temporality dimension is absent.

Lin et al. [44] provide a dedicated survey of agent memory security, the deepest treatment of L3 in the literature. Our work incorporates their taxonomy and extends it by situating L3 threats within the cross-layer context and connecting them to T3 temporality. They do not cover other LASM layers.

Hou et al. [13] conduct a targeted security analysis of the MCP ecosystem. Their empirical vulnerability statistics are highly cited in our L6 analysis. Their scope is narrower: L6 only, no temporality, no multi-agent or memory analysis.

MITRE ATLAS [38] and OWASP LLM Top 10 [37] are the most widely deployed practitioner-facing frameworks for AI security. MITRE ATLAS organizes AI attacks by Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs), analogous to MITRE ATT&CK for enterprise systems. OWASP LLM Top 10 enumerates the ten most critical vulnerabilities in LLM applications by exploitability and business impact. These frameworks answer the question “what is the attacker doing?” and are TTP-centric. LASM answers the complementary question: “where in the system architecture is the control point?” The two approaches are orthogonal and mutually reinforcing: an ATLAS technique such as “Prompt Injection” maps to LASM’s L4 layer; “Model Backdoor” maps to L1 and L6. Practitioners can use ATLAS TTPs to identify attacker behaviors and LASM to determine where defenses should be placed. Neither ATLAS nor OWASP LLM Top 10 incorporates a temporal dimension or addresses the higher-layer threats (L5–L7) that this survey identifies as under-studied.

Foundational work on security and privacy in ML [144, 58] established the threat taxonomy for classical ML systems; this survey extends that foundation to the agentic setting, where the attack surface encompasses not just the model but the entire reasoning-memory-tool-coordination stack. Collectively, prior work provides deep coverage of individual attack types (ATLAS, OWASP) or individual architectural layers (Lin et al. [44], Hou et al. [13]), but no prior work provides: (a) a unified architectural framework spanning all seven layers with formal layer boundaries; (b) a temporal dimension for classifying when attacks manifest; (c) a cross-layer defense taxonomy covering temporal coverage; or (d) systematic identification of the high-risk, under-studied zone at {L5–L7} ×\times {T3–T4}.

XVI Conclusion

AI agents are deployed in production systems managing enterprise files, executing financial transactions, writing and deploying code, and coordinating complex multi-step workflows on behalf of millions of users. Their security is a societal concern, not merely a technical one.

The central argument of this survey is that agentic AI security requires its own analytical framework. Borrowing from stateless LLM safety or traditional software security leaves the most dangerous threats unaddressed. The Layered Attack Surface Model (LASM) provides a seven-layer decomposition that assigns each threat class to the architectural component that must defend against it. The attack temporality dimension shows that the threats with the highest real-world impact are not instantaneous attacks at well-studied layers, but slow-burning, high-layer attacks that existing defenses and benchmarks leave unmeasured.

Through a systematic review of 94 papers, we documented the state of the art across all seven layers, proposed a cross-layer defense taxonomy, surveyed evaluation benchmarks and their gaps, and identified five research gaps: Gap 1 (cross-session attack benchmarks), Gap 2 (emergent misalignment detection), Gap 3 (steganographic collusion detection), Gap 4 (ABOM standardization and MCP certification), and Gap 5 (system-level accountability frameworks).

Agent security is a distributed systems problem embedded in an adversarial ecosystem, not a model problem, not a prompt problem, and not a challenge amenable to better safety training alone. Of the five gaps identified in Section XIII, Gaps 1, 4, and 5 offer the clearest path to near-term engineering progress; Gaps 2 and 3 have no short-term solution path.

Gaps 1, 4, 5 (near-term tractable). Gap 1 (multi-session evaluation infrastructure) is prerequisite to measuring progress on all slow-burn threats. Cross-session replay infrastructure, memory state serialization, and ground-truth labeling are engineering problems for which the necessary components already exist; they have not been assembled for the security evaluation use case. Gap 4 (ABOM standardization and MCP security certification) is an engineering coordination problem rather than a research problem, tractable in the near term and with disproportionate risk-reduction value, analogous to how SBOM adoption transformed software supply-chain security after NTIA mandated it. Gap 5 (system-level accountability frameworks) spans formal trajectory attribution, mandatory action logging, and legal liability allocation; it is a prerequisite for deploying agents in high-stakes domains regardless of whether the other gaps are solved.

Gaps 2 and 3 (fundamental open problems). Emergent misalignment detection (Gap 2) and general steganographic collusion detection (Gap 3) have no near-term solution path: both require detecting statistical anomalies in high-dimensional stochastic distributions, and both face adversaries who can adapt to known detection methods. Sustained basic research is required before engineering progress is tractable. The intellectual foundations exist across statistical process control, information theory, formal verification, and distributed systems; the work is their adaptation to the specific distributional and behavioral properties of agentic AI systems.

Limitations

This survey has four limitations. First, the corpus was coded by a single author; the conservative ambiguity rule in Section II and the per-cell citations in Table V mitigate but do not replace formal inter-rater reliability assessment, which remains future work. Second, coverage ends April 2025; the field publishes rapidly and some recent work is missing. Third, LASM organizes threats by architectural layer, but agent deployments vary; an agent without persistent memory has no L3 attack surface, and the framework should be applied to the actual deployment configuration. Fourth, the MCP vulnerability statistics from [13] come from an unreviewed preprint; the directional findings are consistent with independently documented incidents, but the exact percentages are not peer-validated.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
